qrdBas-ae9495-d1e101.summary: Rubric for the fourth prologue (introductory) question of Book 1.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e108.summary: States the question: whether God is the subject of theology under the proper ratio of deity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e117.summary: First argument for the negative: a special science should have its subject under a special, contracted ratio, as a common science under a general one; deity is not a contracted but rather an absolute ratio.
claims: A special science requires a contracted ratio of its subject.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e135.summary: Second argument: the noblest science should have its subject under the noblest ratio, which is goodness, not deity, since good and end are the same (Metaphysics II) and, per Avicenna (Metaphysics VI), a science of the end would be noblest.
claims: The noblest ratio is goodness or the end.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e154.summary: Third argument: a formally infinite ratio cannot be the objective ratio of a finite science, since sciences are named and perfected by their objects, so a finite science would be infinite; deity is formally infinite.
claims: A formally infinite objective ratio would make a finite science infinite.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e170.summary: Fourth argument: God cannot be object of uncreated and of created science under the same ratio, for there would be no proportion between sciences and objects; God under deity is the object of his own science.
claims: Created and uncreated science must have objects under different rationes.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e181.summary: Confirmation from authorities: Hugh of St Victor (De sacramentis) makes the works of restoration theology's subject, so God as restorer or glorifier; Cassiodorus makes it the whole Christ, head and members, so God as incarnate head of the Church. The last words begin the counter-argument.
claims: Some authorities assign theology's subject under a relational or economic ratio.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e197.summary: For the affirmative: knowledge of something under a contracted ratio presupposes knowledge under the absolute ratio, as optics presupposes geometry of the line; so if God were subject under a contracted ratio, theology would presuppose a prior science of God, which is false.
claims: Knowledge under a contracted ratio presupposes knowledge under the absolute ratio.
No science of God is prior to theology.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e232.summary: Second step: argue against them, presenting another view that pleases more.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e237.summary: Third step: respond to their reasons.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e242.summary: Fourth step: inquire whether theology concerns all things by attribution to God under the ratio of deity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e249.summary: Fifth step: respond to the specific arguments. The paragraph's last words begin the first article.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e256.summary: First article: an opinion that God under deity is not theology's subject. First proof: God under deity is the subject of one part of metaphysics (Book XII); two sciences of the same object under the same ratio can be had in the same light, given the correspondence of habits, lights, and objects; so if metaphysics is had in natural light, theology would be too, which is false.
claims: Sciences of the same object under the same ratio can be had in the same light.
God under deity is the subject of Metaphysics XII.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e282.summary: Second proof: when an object under its proper ratio contains all things, a science of it under that ratio extends to them all; God under deity contains everything, intrinsic and extrinsic, under their proper rationes; so theology would extend to infinitely many knowables and be infinite.
claims: A science of God under deity would extend to infinitely many objects and be infinite.
concepts: containment of all things in God

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e305.summary: Confirmation: if deity or any formally infinite ratio were the formal object of theology or the beatific vision, the created act would be intensively infinite; since acts are ennobled by objects and there is no infinite regress of species, the vision would exceed any act about creatures infinitely and be nobler than infinitely many acts, and so actually infinite. The same holds of fruition. Possible replies: the act would be nobler than infinitely many acts without containing them perfectionally or exceeding each disproportionately; or greater nobility of object does not always produce commensurate nobility of science, which holds only of infinite object and uncreated science.
claims: A formally infinite object would seem to make the created act intensively infinite.
Created knowledge need not be commensurate with the nobility of its object.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e370.summary: Third proof: the objective ratio of a science follows the demand of its end; theology's end is love or charity, which regards the good, so its ratio is goodness, not deity. Fourth: objects never exceed the light of the corresponding knowledge (as with sight), but deity, simply infinite, exceeds any light in us, natural or infused.
claims: Theology's objective ratio follows its end, charity, which regards the good.
An infinite ratio exceeds every created light.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e405.summary: The opinion concludes that deity cannot be the formal ratio of theology's object; another must be assigned.
claims: Deity cannot be the formal objective ratio of theology.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e412.summary: On the alternatives there are as many opinions as heads: some say God is theology's subject under the ratio of goodness or end.
claims: Some assign goodness or end as the subject's ratio.
Some assign God's work of glorification or restoration as the ratio.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e426.summary: Others: under a finite ratio posited in God by the nature of things, though materially or fundamentally infinite, object of the blessed's knowledge and of theology, since they cannot see how a formally finite knowledge could have a formally infinite object.
claims: Some posit a formally finite ratio in God as the object of created knowledge.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e440.summary: One doctor in his Quodlibet holds God is object of his own science under infinity, as formal ratio, but of created science under the ratio of his essence, with infinity only concomitant, moved by the last three reasons. Others say: under the ratio of the credible, since theology nourishes and defends faith, whose object is the credible.
claims: God is object of his own knowledge under infinity but of created knowledge under essence.
Some assign the credible as theology's ratio.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e466.summary: Others: under the ratio of the non-apparent, since theology is not evident from its object.
claims: Some assign non-apparentness as theology's ratio.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e471.summary: Others, like Thomas (Summa I q.1): as supernaturally revealed, to save theology's truth. Yet Thomas also says God under deity is the subject, since all things are attributed and reduced to him, so he seems inconsistent. The author announces arguments against all these opinions.
claims: Aquinas assigns both revealability and deity, which seems inconsistent.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e489.summary: Against goodness (as distinct from essence or deity): the first science simply regards its object under the first ratio, not a secondary one; theology generically is the first and highest science; goodness is secondary and posterior to divine entity or deity.
claims: The first science regards its object under the first ratio.
Goodness is posterior to deity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e513.summary: Further: goodness is like an attribute relative to some prior ratio in God, so it cannot be the ratio of the first subject; else a prior science regarding that prior ratio would precede theology.
claims: An attributal ratio presupposes a prior ratio and a prior science.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e526.summary: Further: knowledge of what a thing is is most perfect and first (Metaphysics VII), so the quidditative ratio is the ratio of the first object. Goodness or any attributal ratio distinct from deity is not God's quiddity. Just as the highest science of man would not treat him under a general ratio (confused), an attribute (presupposing quidditative science), or a relation or negation (presupposing the foundation), but under his quiddity, so here.
claims: The ratio of the first object is quidditative.
No attributal or relational ratio is God's quiddity.
concepts: analogy of the science of man

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e558.summary: Hence no ratio common by predication can be theology's objective ratio, since none virtually contains theological truths, theology would be confused, and common rationes are not naturally known to God alone. Nor can any attributal or posterior ratio, since such rationes are ordered to the first, however distinguished, as if really distinct, and a posterior ratio cannot be the first objective ratio of the first science.
claims: Neither common nor attributal rationes can be theology's objective ratio.
Distinct rationes in God are ordered as if really distinct.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e597.summary: Second: God is not theology's subject under the ratio of glorifier, credible, lovable, head, restorer, or revealable, or any relation of reason to creatures. A science considering its subject through a relation of reason is a science of reason, not real, like logic. God's relations to creatures are of reason only, and a being of reason is not formally in God, being diminished and most imperfect.
claims: A science whose objective ratio is a relation of reason is a rational, not real, science.
God's relations to creatures are relations of reason.
No being of reason is formally in God.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e628.summary: Further: no such ratio makes a per se unified concept with God, only an accidental unity like a being of reason with a real being; so theology would be merely a rational science, or would presuppose two others about the parts of that accidentally unified concept.
claims: Relational rationes make only accidental unity with God.
concepts: per se and per accidens unity

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e644.summary: If these rationes signify not relations of reason but their foundation, the author has his point: God is subject under deity, since in that sense God is credible and glorifier with deity as the foundation of these relations.
claims: Taken as foundation, these rationes reduce to deity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e662.summary: Third: the non-apparent cannot be theology's formal objective ratio, since a negation, being formally non-being, cannot be the first formal objective ratio of something positive, and there is no science of non-being (Posterior Analytics I). Theology is a positive habit.
claims: A negation cannot be the formal object of a positive habit.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e678.summary: Further: a negation is known only through an affirmation, so it cannot be the first formal objective ratio of any knowledge. The paragraph ends by introducing the next proof.
claims: Negations are known only through affirmations.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e688.summary: Fourth: God is not subject under a finite ratio in him by the nature of things. Such a ratio is fictitious and impossible, since God is infinite and nothing finite can be in him by the nature of things, except in relation to creatures, as some say of ideas.
claims: Nothing finite can be in God by the nature of things.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e706.summary: Further: if a finite ratio were evidently known, the necessary theological truths would not be evident, since it cannot virtually include, in concept or effect, that God is triune and one, a truth all doctors resolve to divine infinity, holding it impossible of anything limited.
claims: A finite ratio cannot virtually contain the Trinity.
The Trinity is resolved to divine infinity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e726.summary: Further: by parity, a finite ratio would be the object of beatitude, which is finite; but no one is beatified by a finite ratio, since the beatifiable power rests only in an object containing all secondary objects perfectionally or virtually, and beyond any finite object one can desire more. So none of the opinions holds. Ends the first article.
claims: No finite ratio can beatify, since desire extends beyond any finite object.
None of the alternative opinions is true.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e757.summary: Second article, the author's answer: distinguishing necessary from contingent theology, for necessary theology (God's, the blessed's, or wayfarers') God is the per se first subject under the proper ratio of his essence, which is deity.
claims: God is the subject of necessary theology under the ratio of deity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e775.summary: First proof: God is theology's subject under the ratio by which he first virtually contains all its truths; that is deity, the simply first and quidditative ratio, others being posterior quasi-attributes.
claims: Deity is the quidditative ratio virtually containing all theological truths.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e793.summary: Second proof: God is object of his own intellect under the same ratio (to be shown at d5 or d7).
claims: God's own intellect has deity as object.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e801.summary: Third proof: God is subject under the ratio by which he exceeds in knowability everything else considered in theology, which is deity alone.
claims: Deity is the ratio by which God exceeds all in knowability.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e810.summary: Fourth proof: God is subject under the ratio under which all else in theology is best attributed and reduced to him, which is deity.
claims: All theological objects are best reduced to God under deity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e821.summary: A fifth reason from that doctor (deity is more actual than goodness because less communicable) the author does not understand: divine goodness is no more communicable than deity, both being communicable and infinite on the doctor's own view; and if less communicable meant more actual, relation would be more actual than goodness or deity, which is false, since relation, on his view, is neither finite nor infinite.
claims: Communicability does not measure actuality.
Relation is not more actual than absolute perfections.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e852.summary: The author keeps the preceding reasons and adds a sixth: God is subject under the ratio through which theological properties are chiefly denominated of him and through whose evident knowledge their inherence is first evident, which is deity alone.
claims: Deity is the ratio through which theological properties are known to belong to God.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e868.summary: Note: the concept of deity, the formal ratio under which God is subject, must be in God by the nature of things, distinct from attributal rationes prior to any act of intellect. A real science's proper formal ratio must be real, else it would be a being of reason. The intellect cannot fabricate a quidditative concept of God, nor can the divine object move a power to cause one. So it is nothing to say the intellect makes diverse concepts of God, one quidditative and others attributal, since any concept made by the intellect is a being of reason, not God. Since propter quid science requires an order of the quidditative concept to others, not from the act (God knows by one simple act), the order must be in the object, so there is a distinction from the nature of things in God.
claims: The formal ratio of deity is in God from the nature of things, distinct from attributes.
No intellect-made concept can be quidditative of God.
Demonstrative science of God requires a real order of rationes in God, hence a formal distinction.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e938.summary: On contingent theology (God's, the blessed's, or wayfarers'), two ways can be taken, as in the previous question.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e948.summary: First way (that doctor's): God under deity is subject of contingent theology as of necessary, but not uniformly. For contingent theology he is not an object determinately containing its truths or their evidence, but the first intuitable proximate to that in which the first contingent predicate inheres. For necessary theology, at least God's and the blessed's, he virtually contains its truths and their evidence.
claims: God under deity is subject of contingent theology only as first intuitable proximate to the will.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e977.summary: Second way: God's essence taken absolutely cannot be subject of contingent theology, since it does not determinately contain contingent truths. As will under its actual determination, it does. The act of determination is not part of the subject's ratio (it is the predicate of the first contingent truth), but the will must stand under it for contingent truths to be determinately and certainly contained. Through the first immediate contingent complex, known only in itself, the others can be known with certainty.
claims: The divine will under its actual determination is the first subject of contingent theology.
The first immediate contingent truth is knowable only in itself.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1021.summary: Resolves: if 'subject' means what first occurs to knowledge, God under deity is subject of contingent theology. If it means what first determinately contains its truths, the divine essence or deity falls short taken absolutely; the will under its determining act must concur, or one waits for a 'third instant' in which the essence under deity represents the determination made by the will in the second instant and so contains contingent truths in intelligible being. Any of the three ways is probable. So God under deity is the subject of theology.
claims: Under one sense of 'subject', God under deity is subject of contingent theology.
For determinate containment of contingents, the will's determination must concur, or the essence represents it at a later instant.
God is theology's subject under the proper ratio of deity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1067.summary: Introduces replies to the arguments of the contrary opinion.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1072.summary: Reply to the first: God can be subject under deity of both Metaphysics XII and theology. It does not follow that both can be had in the same light, any more than faith and vision (both about God) can, given the diverse natures of the knowledges. The correspondence of objects and lights is not that same object requires same light or same habit, but that the same object is intelligible through each habit in its corresponding light. Also, the argument would make metaphysics infinite, extending to all things distinctly and perfectly.
claims: Sciences about the same object under the same ratio need not share the same light.
The same object can be known through different habits in different lights.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1107.summary: Reply to the second: when an object extends to all things, the science of it need not extend to all in every intellect, only in an intellect adequate to the object's intelligibility, which is the divine intellect alone. On the side of the receiving subject the science is limited, so one knower can draw more conclusions from the same principle than another; the object can exceed the science as its equivocal cause, but the science cannot exceed the object. The argument would also deny being as metaphysics' subject. A created intellect can know all things and God himself distinctly by supernatural means, though not as perfectly or naturally as God.
claims: A science's extension is limited by the receiving intellect, not only by its object.
The object can exceed the science, but the science cannot exceed the object.
A created intellect can supernaturally know all things and God distinctly, though less perfectly than God.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1163.summary: Reply to the third: deity is the ratio appropriate to theology's end even if its end is charitable love, since God under deity is first lovable, naturally and with charity. Goodness, as to anything positive outside the intellect, is not distinct from deity; it is either wholly the same really and formally, or differs only by reason or by some negation, neither of which can be the primary objective ratio of a positive habit or act.
claims: God under deity is first lovable by charity.
Goodness is not positively distinct from deity outside the intellect.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1192.summary: Reply to the fourth: an object never so exceeds the habit concerning it that it cannot be attained in some way in the corresponding light, though not adequately and perfectly. The example of sight cuts against the opponent too, since he posits many things understood about God not in the intellect's natural light.
claims: An object can be attained in a light without being adequately grasped.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1212.summary: Sight cannot see anything beyond its natural light because of its limitation and narrowness, but the intellect, a power unlimited to all beings, can attain many things it cannot reach naturally or perfectly; objects exceed both the power and any light that can be infused into it. Perhaps only natural light is necessarily required on the side of knowability. Ends the second article.
claims: The intellect, unlike sight, is unlimited in scope and can attain objects exceeding its light.
Objects can exceed every light infusible into the intellect.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1245.summary: Third article: whether theology concerns all things by attribution to God under deity. Theology is threefold: God's, the blessed's, and the wayfarers'.
claims: Theology is threefold: God's, the blessed's, and the wayfarers'.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1261.summary: On God's theology, an objection: it does not concern all knowables through deity, since many truths are contained first in created quiddities (a triangle would have three angles and man risibility even if, per impossibile, God did not exist), and what does not first contain a truth cannot be the ratio of knowing it, so God knows some truths about things through their proper quiddities.
claims: Some truths are first contained in created quiddities, independently of God.
God would know such truths through the quiddities themselves.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1294.summary: Against it: if the divine intellect were moved to knowledge by anything extrinsic, such as created quiddities, it would depend on something extrinsic and not be simply first and independent; since his understanding is his essence, he would not be God and his intellect would be debased. He would wait, after understanding his essence, to be moved by the line, in passive potency, and would have really distinct intellections.
claims: The divine intellect cannot be moved by anything extrinsic to it.
Dependence on created quiddities would make God's intellect passive and composite.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1334.summary: Further: a power actuated by diverse objects by their own virtue has as first object something common to them, not one of them; if each thing could cause knowledge in God by its own power, the divine intellect's first object would be something common to it and others, which is false. Attribution of everything to the essence does not suffice, as accidents are attributed to substance without substance being the intellect's adequate object.
claims: If God's intellect were moved by many objects, its first object would be a common ratio, not his essence.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1369.summary: Further: the divine essence is first object not by predicative community but by virtual containment of others; if each quiddity moved the divine intellect, the essence would not be first by containment.
claims: The essence is first object of the divine intellect by virtual containment.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1389.summary: Further: new intellection would arise in God, since quiddities not existing from eternity could not move him from eternity; so he would change and not be pure act. Conclusion: God's theology concerns all knowables through deity. In a first instant (by our mode of understanding) the essence causes knowledge of itself, in a second knowledge of all created quiddities it virtually contains, and in a third knowledge of all truths contained in them. These are three quasi-effects from one principle in an order of reason, not caused by the quiddities. If the essence's motion stopped at the first instant, God could never know created quiddities or their truths.
claims: God would change if moved by created objects.
God knows all through his essence in an ordered sequence of instants: himself, quiddities, truths.
Created quiddities do not cause knowledge in God.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1452.summary: Brief transitional note: so much for God's theology concerning necessary truths.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1457.summary: On God's theology of contingents, refers to the previous question. God has only theological knowledge of all things, and his theology is all his knowledge, since it alone includes no limitation or imperfection and contains all knowledge possible to him through his essence.
claims: All of God's knowledge is theology.
God's theology includes no limitation.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1477.summary: Against others' motive (that many truths are not first and immediately contained in the essence): this is not required for God's theological knowledge of them; it suffices that the essence contains them through created quiddities, though it would be required for proper and distinct knowledge of them in their own genus. Or the mediation of quiddities is not causal, and God contains the truths as immediately as the quiddities.
claims: God's theological knowledge of truths can be mediated by quiddities.
Quiddities do not mediate causally between God and truths.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1502.summary: Better: the divine essence first contains such truths as first cause, containing even truths that follow attributes. To the counterfactual (if God did not exist the quiddities would still contain them), one can retort that God contained them from eternity when the quiddities did not exist. The counterfactual posits incompossibles, since if God did not exist the quiddities would exist neither really nor intelligibly, since they first have intelligible being through divine intellection, and so would contain nothing.
claims: The divine essence first contains all truths as first cause.
Created quiddities have intelligible being only through divine intellection.
The counterfactual of God's non-existence posits incompossibles.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1537.summary: On the blessed's theology: since the same act knows the divine essence and whatever it naturally represents, it concerns all quiddities and necessary complexes through the ratio of the essence, whether finite or infinite. Seeing the essence clearly without seeing all it necessarily represents is inconceivable, since knowing extensive infinity is no greater than knowing intensive infinity. If the acts were distinct (which he doubts), God could cause the first without the second.
claims: The blessed, in one act, know the essence and all it necessarily represents.
Knowing extensive infinity is no greater than knowing intensive infinity.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1579.summary: Rejects the view that the divine essence is a voluntary object for the blessed and need not represent everything. It is voluntary as to God's influence on the act, but once the act is posited all that the essence necessarily represents is seen, since it is one act. Yet the blessed's theology is not all their knowledge: they also know things in their own genus, moved by external objects, with evening as well as morning knowledge. So a doctor's distinction (theology of the blessed in itself versus as had by a finite intellect, limited de facto by God's will) is beside the point; in every sense it concerns all the necessary truths mentioned.
claims: Once the beatific act is posited, all that the essence necessarily represents is seen.
The blessed also have knowledge of things in their own genus (evening knowledge).
The blessed's theology concerns all necessary truths, in itself and as they have it.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1649.summary: The blessed's theology of contingents need not concern all; they do not know many contingents, about which revelations can be made, and they know no contingent complex through deity by knowing the Word, since then they would know all in the same act. The essence represents contingents only in the 'third instant', not the first, so any contingents they know through it are by other, varied acts. Wayfarers' theology, revealed or derived from revelation, concerns only what is revealed in Scripture and what necessarily follows from it (Apocalypse 22: whoever adds, God will add plagues).
claims: The blessed do not know all contingents and know none through deity in the beatific act.
Our theology concerns only Scripture and what follows necessarily from it.
concepts: knowledge of contingents by the blessed

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1697.summary: Second, our theology cannot concern all things, because our intellect in this state cannot grasp the quiddities of all terms. Revelation by common law concerns only complexes whose terms we can naturally conceive, revealing the truth of complexes, not concepts of terms. It concerns other things only under a general ratio (all things are produced by God). Some add that our theology cannot coexist with evident knowledge, but that was refuted: revealed theology can coexist with naturally known truths (that God is one, omnipotent), else theologians learning demonstrations would lose faith and merit, which is absurd. Ends the third article.
claims: Revelation by common law concerns the truth of complexes, not new concepts of terms.
Our theology treats creatures only under a general ratio.
Revealed theology can coexist with demonstrations of the same truths.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1749.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: a special science does have a special objective ratio. Deity is most special and contracted, as opposed to what is universal by predication, which suffices, though not contracted for knowledge as posterior rationes are; that would be impossible.
claims: Deity is the most special ratio as opposed to predicative universality.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1770.summary: Reply to the second: deity is the ratio of the noblest end, implying foundation and a relation of reason of God to effects; goodness and deity are the same in their positive content outside the intellect.
claims: Deity and goodness are positively the same; deity is the ratio of the noblest end.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1786.summary: Reply to the third: not every perfection or property of an object denominates the science, as a science of stone is not called stony, hard, or corporeal. So a science about the infinite, under an infinite ratio, need not be formally infinite, which is repugnant to it, at least for those who deny an actually intensively infinite creature; and even if possible, it need not be.
claims: Not every perfection of an object denominates the science.
A science of the infinite need not be formally infinite.

qrdBas-ae9495-d1e1817.summary: Reply to the fourth: God is subject of his own and of created science under the same intrinsically infinite ratio, deity. The proportion of object and science is not equality of perfection but such as suffices for one to be knowledge of the other. To Hugh and Cassiodorus: they speak of theology's matter considered by attribution to the formal object, not of its first formal object.
claims: God is object of divine and created science under the same ratio.
Proportion between object and science does not require equal perfection.
Works of restoration and the whole Christ are matter of theology by attribution, not its formal object.

qrdBas-ae9495.summary: Prologue q4 asks whether God is theology's subject under the proper ratio of deity. Against an opinion that denies this (deity being metaphysics' subject, infinite, exceeding any light, and not the ratio of theology's end, charity), and against alternative rationes (goodness, glorifier or restorer, a finite ratio in God, the credible, the non-apparent, the supernaturally revealed, whose proponents include Aquinas), Bassolis argues that deity is the ratio. Goodness and other attributes are posterior quasi-attributes; the first science regards the quidditative ratio. Relational rationes are relations of reason that would make theology a rational science like logic. Negations cannot specify a positive habit. Nothing finite is in God, and no finite ratio could contain the Trinity or beatify. Deity is the subject of necessary theology because it virtually contains all theological truths, exceeds all in knowability, and grounds all attribution. This requires that deity be distinct from attributal rationes 'from the nature of things' (a formal distinction), since no intellect-made concept can be quidditative of God. For contingent theology, God under deity is subject as what first occurs, but determinate containment needs the will under its determination, or the essence representing it at a 'third instant'. In the third article he treats theology's scope. God's theology covers all knowables through his essence in an ordered sequence (essence, quiddities, truths), since God cannot be moved by created quiddities, which have intelligible being only from him. The blessed see in one act all that the essence necessarily represents, but not contingents, and also have evening knowledge in the proper genus. Our theology is limited to Scripture and its necessary consequences, reveals complexes rather than new concepts, and can coexist with demonstration. He replies that a science of the infinite need not be infinite, and that the proportion of science to object need not be equality.
claims: God is theology's subject under the proper ratio of deity, not goodness, relation, negation, revealability, or any finite ratio.
Deity is the quidditative ratio that virtually contains all theological truths.
The ratio of deity is distinct from attributes from the nature of things, prior to any act of intellect.
God's knowledge is caused wholly by his essence in an order of instants, never by created objects.
The blessed see in one act all that the divine essence necessarily represents, but not contingents.
Our theology extends only to Scripture and what follows necessarily from it.
